desc:
The arrays nums1 and nums2 hold decimal digits (values 0 to 9). Build a sequence of exactly k digits by choosing some digits from nums1 and some from nums2 (possibly none from one of them). The chosen digits from each array must keep their relative order from that array, but digits of the two arrays may be interleaved in any way.

Return the digit sequence that, read as a number, is the largest. All candidates have exactly k digits, so this is the lexicographically largest sequence.

Example: nums1 = [3, 4, 6, 5], nums2 = [9, 1, 2, 5, 8, 3], k = 5 gives [9, 8, 6, 5, 3].
hints: If you knew how many digits i come from nums1 (and k - i from nums2), the problem would split into two simpler ones. Try every feasible i.

For a single array, the best subsequence of length t is found with a monotonic stack: drop smaller digits in front of a larger digit while you still have spare deletions (the 'remove k digits' idea, maximizing instead of minimizing).

Merge two chosen subsequences greedily: at each step take the next digit from the sequence whose remaining suffix is lexicographically larger (not just the larger next digit, ties must be broken by looking further). Compare all i results and keep the largest.
editorial: Split by the number of digits taken from the first array. For each feasible i (from max(0, k - len(nums2)) to min(k, len(nums1))), take the best length-i subsequence of nums1 and the best length-(k-i) subsequence of nums2. The best subsequence of a single array is found by a monotonic stack that pops a smaller digit when a larger one arrives and deletions are still available (at most len - t of them).

Then merge the two subsequences into the largest sequence. At each step compare the remaining parts of the two sequences as lists (the comparison of suffixes, not only of their first digits, because equal leading digits must be resolved by looking further) and take the head of the larger one. The best result over all i is the answer. Choosing the subsequences independently is safe because merging cannot reorder digits inside a subsequence, and the optimal final sequence uses the optimal subsequence of each array for its own counts. Complexity is O(k * (m + n)) for the stacks plus O(k) merges per split, each merge costing up to O(k) in comparisons; with m, n ≤ 200 this is tiny.
time: O(k * (m + n) * k) worst case, small for m, n ≤ 200
